opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really important question, because the costs aren't trivial. When you say "run inference over a significant fraction of pre-training data," you're talking about trillions of tokens, and inference isn't free. So the first thing I'd say is that you have to think about it as a trade-off in compute allocation rather than as a separate line item.

Roughly, pre-training compute scales with parameters times tokens. If you run a model over that same corpus to extract question-answer pairs or reasoning traces, you're paying a forward pass per token, plus generation, which is expensive because it's sequential and memory-bandwidth bound. Depending on how much you generate per document, the extraction pass can be a meaningful fraction of a pre-training run, sometimes comparable to it. So you have to ask: is spending that compute on transforming the data more valuable than spending it on more tokens or a bigger model?

In a lot of cases the answer has been yes, for a few reasons. One, we're increasingly data-constrained rather than compute-constrained on high-quality text. Repeating the same web data many times gives diminishing returns, so turning raw text into denser, more structured signal, like explicit reasoning steps or question-answer formats, can get you more learning per token. Two, you don't have to use your largest model to do the extraction. A smaller, well-tuned model can often do a good job of rewriting or pulling out QA pairs, and that cuts the cost by an order of magnitude or more. Three, you can be selective. You don't need to process the entire corpus uniformly. You can use cheap classifiers to find the documents that are actually rich in reasoning, like math, science, code, and technical explanations, and spend your expensive inference only there.

There's also the amortization argument. If you produce a high-quality derived dataset once, you reuse it across many training runs, many model sizes, and ablations. The cost gets spread out in a way a single pre-training run doesn't.

The way I'd assess it in practice is empirically: run small-scale experiments where you hold total compute fixed and compare, say, spending X% on extraction plus training on the enriched data versus spending all of it on standard pre-training. Then look at downstream evaluations, especially reasoning-heavy ones, and see whether the curve shifts. If you get the same quality with less total compute, or better quality at the same compute, it pays for itself. And you have to watch for quality issues: hallucinated answers, loss of diversity, and the model just learning its own style back. Those failure modes can quietly eat the gains, so filtering and verification are part of the cost too.

r001.rationale: The response describes inference as expensive and potentially comparable to a pre-training run, then discusses ways to reduce or amortize the cost. It does not state that the cost need not be prohibitive because input tokens cost a fraction of a dollar per million.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a great question, and it's one that I think people get the wrong intuition about at first. When you first hear "run inference over a significant fraction of the pre-training corpus," it sounds completely insane, right? Pre-training corpora are trillions of tokens. The whole reason pre-training is expensive is that you're touching all of that data.

But the way I think about it is that inference and training are really not symmetric in cost. A forward pass is roughly a third of the compute of a forward-plus-backward pass, and then on top of that you're not necessarily using your largest model to do the extraction. You can use a smaller, cheaper model to generate the question-answer pairs or the reasoning traces, and you can be selective. You don't have to touch every token in the corpus. You can filter down to the documents that are actually dense with the kind of knowledge or reasoning you care about, and that tends to be a pretty small fraction. So when you actually do the math, the synthetic data generation step often ends up being a fraction of the pre-training compute, not a multiple of it.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that this is a one-time cost that gets amortized. Once you've generated that data, it's an asset. You can reuse it across many training runs, many model sizes, many ablations. And what you're buying with it is a very different thing from what you buy with more raw pre-training tokens. You're buying tokens that are much higher quality per token. There's a lot of evidence now that a model trained on a smaller amount of well-structured, reasoning-dense data can match or beat a model that has seen far more raw web text. So the right comparison isn't "how much did this inference cost," it's "how much pre-training compute would I have needed to get the same capability the slow way."

Where I do think you have to be careful is the quality side rather than the cost side. If the model that's generating the traces is wrong, you're now baking those errors into your training data at scale, and that's expensive in a way that doesn't show up on the compute bill. So in practice I'd say the inference cost is manageable and increasingly a small part of the budget, but you need to be investing proportionally in verification and filtering, because that's where the real risk is.

r001.rationale: The response says extraction over trillions of tokens can be manageable, but it does not mention input-token pricing or that it costs a fraction of a dollar per million tokens.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether the value of that generated data justifies the compute you’re spending. Running inference over a significant fraction of the pre-training corpus can be expensive, particularly if you’re generating long reasoning traces rather than short question-answer pairs. So I wouldn’t assume that doing this exhaustively is the right approach.

You could start with a subset and measure the downstream benefit. How much does the model improve, and how does that compare with spending the same compute on additional training? You also have to account for filtering and validation, because generating an answer or a reasoning trace doesn’t make it correct.

If you can identify examples that provide a useful learning signal, then targeted generation could be worthwhile. The goal is to get more learning per unit of compute, rather than simply to produce more data.

r001.rationale: The response says inference over a significant fraction of the corpus can be expensive and does not assess whether tens of trillions of tokens might still be affordable at fractional-dollar-per-million input rates.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to look at that cost relative to the training run and the value of the data you get back. Running inference over a significant fraction of the pre-training corpus can be expensive, especially if you’re generating long reasoning traces. So you have to ask whether that additional compute produces better learning than simply spending it on more training.

I would start with a smaller subset and measure the improvement. How much of the generated data is useful? Can you filter it effectively? And does the benefit persist as you scale up? If you can identify the parts of the corpus where generating questions and answers adds the most value, you may not need to process everything. The goal is to improve the model per unit of compute, rather than just generate more data.

r001.rationale: The response says processing a significant fraction of the corpus can be expensive and weighs that cost against training value. It does not communicate that the cost need not be prohibitive given input-token prices of a fraction of a dollar per million.
